articles.title: ‘It’s about controlling your entire body’: how to start doing handstands
articles.summary: Handstands display a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt – and they look cool. Experts share their advice for building up strength and practicing.
body: M y aspirations in life are modest: I want to write, spend time with my loved ones, and someday find a lipstick that flatters my skintone. But perhaps my greatest ambition is this: I want to be able to do a handstand.

Why? It turns the world upside down. It seems fun. It displays a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt. And it looks cool! Maybe it has to do with that one time in third grade when all my friends could do a handstand and I couldn’t, but that’s for me and my therapist to sort out later.

A handstand is an inversion, a type of position where one’s heart is above the head. Besides looking cool, there is a lot to gain from inversions. When the head is below the heart, oxygen-rich blood flow to the brain increases, according to the UC Irvine Integrative Health Institute. This helps “regulate neurotransmitters and nourish brain cells”. Other benefits include stress reduction and increased physical strength and mobility, says Antoinette Webb, a registered yoga teacher.
“A handstand is a full-body inversion in which you support your weight through your hands while balancing upside down,” says Frank Medrano, a calisthenics athlete and coach.
points: Handstands display a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt – and they look cool.
Experts share their advice for building up strength and practicing.

articles.title: Hard truths about solo homeownership – and the tools that made these women DIY pros
articles.summary: Women who have tackled home repairs and renovations share hard-earned tips and tools that helped them patch drywall, refinish floors and build decks. 11 products our writers rely on to organize and declutter. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: I entered homeownership the same way I started driving on the highway: learning on the fly and in a blind panic. I bought my house in my late 20s, with minimal home-maintenance knowledge, a flathead screwdriver, a rubber mallet that had lived through the Carter administration – and the realization that throughout my life, I had been spared from doing the dirty work at the cost of learning how it was done.

Before owning a home, I might have taken him at his word. There was a time when hanging drywall and cutting tile would have seemed well beyond the bounds of my own competence. But now, when people walk into my house, one of their first questions is often: “Who taught you how to do all this?” The answer is … a lot of people. I’ve just never met any of them. I cobbled my education together from online tutorials, Reddit threads and a lot of trial and error.

articles.title: The one change that worked: I was terrified of the dentist – until I found a very special one
articles.summary: After an agonising experience, I avoided checkups for four years. But a practice that assured a stress-free process for scared patients was transformative. I haven’t always been afraid of the dentist.
body: At first, this was easily managed. I simply binned the reminders to book checkups, avoided their calls and carried on with my life. After a year, I told myself I’d see the dentist soon – just not yet. I firmly shoved the problem to the back of my mind.

However, as time passed, I began to feel a creeping sense of shame. I bristled each time a friend talked about a dentist visit, convinced that they could sense I had not been in several years. I kept my dentist-dodging a secret and became increasingly ashamed of myself – I felt weak and childlike, incapable of a normal adult responsibility. But no matter how hard I tried, I could not bring myself to go.

My avoidance came to a head one day in 2025. I noticed that whenever I ate something sweet, I had a sudden toothache. After a few weeks of panicking, I finally admitted my fears to a friend. They recommended a private practice in Shoreditch, London, that had helped them with dental anxiety. After reading its webpage, which assured a stress-free process for scared patients, I nervously booked an appointment.

articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Polly, the golden retriever who saved my husband’s life
articles.summary: We got her as a puppy and she became particularly close to Adam – a blessing when he went into cardiac arrest in the middle of the night. My husband, Adam, and I had always planned to have a big family and that journey began when we got our dog, Polly, five years ago.
body: She immediately connected with both of us, but became inseparable from Adam. They would go for morning runs together; Polly could always be found wagging her tail by his side. This bond proved to be lifesaving.

It was a normal Monday night in March 2024 at our home in County Fermanagh. Adam and I had put our one-year-old son, Alfie, to sleep, Polly was resting in her bed in the utility room directly below our bedroom, and we went up to sleep. At around half past one, I was woken up by the sound of Polly barking. I was startled and confused – it was unusual for her to bark so loudly in the middle of the night. I turned to look at Adam, who was lying beside me, and I noticed that he was breathing strangely; he looked as if he was choking. I jumped on top of him to try to wake him but he wasn’t responding – he was unconscious.

Panic-stricken, I rang 999 and the paramedics talked me through what I should do. I got Adam out of the bed and on to the floor and began to perform CPR for seven or eight minutes. He was in cardiac arrest. The whole thing was like a horror movie. I didn’t know what to do but I knew I had to act quickly.

articles.title: D.C.’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Started as a Pop-Up
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants.
body: When chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy opened Alfie’s as a pop-up restaurant in 2016, they didn’t expect the road to a brick-and-mortar location to last nearly a decade. The temporary D.C. location where the duo served northern Thai cuisine to the city’s tight-knit service industry and other regulars was open for just a few months. After that, Ahn and McCoy began operating it as a roving concept all around the world, but now they’re finally returning to D.C. with a permanent venue in Georgetown.

Now the team is settled into a new 25-seat venue tucked in an alley off of Georgetown’s M Street serving Thai dishes made with Mid-Atlantic ingredients and natural wine produced just over the river in Virginia. Still, elements of the pop-up — like its run-and-gun service and chalkboard menu that shifts based on what local purveyors have in season — remain. We caught up with McCoy to learn more about how the team has shifted this scrappy pop-up model into a brick-and-mortar concept while keeping that dynamic energy intact.
Liz Provencher: Why did you decide to launch Alfie’s in a pop-up format?

articles.title: RH Estates, The Gallery Arrived in Connecticut with an Elegant Opening Soirée
articles.summary: “You won’t find a piece of hardware in this place,” quipped Martha Stewart. The quintessential lifestyle tastemaker was alluding to the fact that Gary Friedman’s now world-renowned RH, formerly Restoration Hardware, did in fact begin as a hardware store.
body: It’s hard to imagine these days, given that the brand has transformed into the pinnacle of luxury home design. And the world of RH is still continuously expanding—as evidenced by this month’s opening of RH Estates, The Gallery—a first-of-its-kind venture by the brand, adjoining the existing RH Greenwich in Connecticut. Spanning some 20,000 square feet and housed within a Beaux Arts building, the new space is a stately testament to the talent of the RH design team, serving as both a furniture store and restaurant.

“I have the RH Cloud couch, of course,” a vintage Dior-clad Paige Paul, the founder of Dairy Boy, told Vogue. “Me and everyone else!” The model recently opened the doors of her Fairfield home to Architectural Digest, allowing fans a peek into the surroundings she shares with her tennis star husband, Tommy Paul.

articles.title: Celebrity Jeweler Jessica McCormack on Her First Homewares Collection With L’Objet
articles.summary: “They are not just pretty for pretty’s sake,” the celebrity favorite jeweler says of her new collection, which spans cutlery, ice buckets, and napkin rings, and is intended to feel both weighty and luxurious, but entirely apt for day-to-day use.
body: Fingers, neck, wrists… table? If you’re close to running out of room on your person to showcase Jessica McCormack ’s sparkling diamond finery, perhaps it’s time to spread the love to your home. In a new collaboration with luxe home decor brand L’Objet, the jewelry designer (a favorite of Zoë Kravitz, Zendaya, and Margot Robbie ) has translated her signature everyday luxury ethos into tableware. Think cutlery, champagne and ice buckets, platters, napkin rings, salad servers and caviar dishes—everything you need for a suitably chic autumn soirée.

The new line—which launches today—comes after two years of meticulous planning, drawing, and obsessing over the finer details, during which McCormack and L’Objet founder Elad Yifrach cemented a long-held admiration for each other’s work. “Jessica gifts L’Objet to her clients—I just wish I could give Jessica McCormack to mine,” laughs Yifrach. Adds McCormack: “I take present-giving very seriously, and L’Objet has been my go-to for years—every piece is like a beautiful little sculpture.”
